title: The seven processes and their purposes
blurb: Recognize the purpose of each of the seven PRINCE2 Agile processes from its hook phrase, and place each one in the project lifecycle.
question: A process exists to answer the question 'Do we have a viable and worthwhile project?'. Which process is it, and how does it differ from initiating a project?

teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile keeps the seven PRINCE2 processes: starting up a project, directing a project, initiating a project, controlling a stage, managing product delivery, managing a stage boundary and closing a project. Each has a fixed purpose; what changes in agile is how the activities are carried out, with agile artifacts such as the release map, project canvas and dashboards, and with named workshops supporting every process.

head: Process
Its purpose in a phrase
rows: Viable and worthwhile? Prerequisites for initiation
Board accountable via key decisions; PM runs day to day
Assign and monitor work, keep the stage within tolerance
Control the link between PM and delivery team
Board reviews the stage, approves the next stage plan
Fixed point: acceptance of the project product confirmed
teach.caption: Purposes paraphrased from 13.2.1 to 13.7.1 and PRINCE2 7 manual 19.1.

teach.h: Before the project: starting up and initiating
teach.body: Starting up a project is triggered by the project mandate (for example a feasibility study, or a request for proposal for a supplier). It makes sure the prerequisites for initiation exist by asking whether the project is viable and worthwhile. Initiating a project then lays solid foundations so the business understands the work needed to deliver the project product before it commits significant money or resources.

levels.label: Business layer
levels.sub: commissions the project; issues the mandate

levels.label: Managing: project manager
levels.sub: SU, initiating, controlling, stage boundary, closing

teach.caption: Starting up also involves the directing level: the business appoints the executive, who appoints the rest of the project management team.

teach.body: Directing a project lets the project board stay accountable for success by taking key decisions and exercising overall control, while delegating day-to-day management to the PM. Controlling a stage is where the PM assigns and monitors work, handles issues, reports progress and takes corrective action to keep the stage within tolerance. Managing product delivery controls the link between the PM and the delivery team: acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery of specialist products.

items.label: Initiating a project, then stage boundary
Controlling a stage + managing product delivery; stage boundary at each end
Controlling, delivering, then closing a project

teach.caption: Controlling a stage can also be used during initiation on large or complex projects.

teach.h: Stage ends and the project end
teach.body: Managing a stage boundary gives the board enough information to review how the current stage went, review the updated release map, approve the next stage plan (an updated release map) and confirm that the business justification and the risks are still acceptable. Closing a project provides a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed and the objectives are recognized as achieved, or the project is closed in an orderly way if it ends early.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.7.1; PRINCE2 7 manual 19.1

teach.body: Fenmoor Water's board issues a mandate for a leak-reporting app. Project manager Priya Nair runs starting up to check the idea is viable and worthwhile, then initiating to agree the release map and approaches before major spend. Executive Tom Hale's board authorizes each stage in directing. Priya assigns sets of user stories in controlling a stage; product owner Kofi Mensah's team delivers them in managing product delivery. At each stage end, Priya updates the release map for the board.

teach.text: Closing a project is NOT a separate stage: it is the last part of the final stage. And do not swap the two early processes: 'viable and worthwhile?' is starting up, while 'solid foundations before significant expenditure' is initiating.

items: Starting up: viable and worthwhile? Triggered by the project mandate.
Directing: board accountable through key decisions; PM handles day to day.
Initiating: solid foundations before significant expenditure.
Controlling a stage: assign, monitor, report, correct within tolerance.
Managing product delivery: the link between PM and delivery team.
Stage boundary: board reviews the stage and approves the updated release map.
Closing: fixed point confirming acceptance of the project product.

summary: You can now state the purpose of each of the seven processes and spot the hook phrase that identifies it. You can also place each process in the lifecycle and say which management level uses it.

A.q: Which process is used to answer the question 'Do we have a viable and worthwhile project?'
A.why: Starting up a project makes sure the prerequisites for initiation are in place by asking whether the project is viable and worthwhile (13.2.1).

whyNot.0: Initiating builds solid foundations before significant expenditure; it follows the decision that the project is worth initiating.
whyNot.2: Directing lets the board make key decisions and keep overall control.
whyNot.3: A stage boundary gives the board information to approve the next stage.

A.q: What is the purpose of the 'managing product delivery' process?
options: To assign work and keep the stage within its tolerances
To give the board information to approve the next stage
To let the board decide while delegating daily control
To control the link between the PM and the delivery team
A.why: Managing product delivery controls the link between the PM and the delivery team by agreeing requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery (13.6.1).

whyNot.0: Assigning work and keeping the stage within tolerance is controlling a stage.
whyNot.1: Informing the board's next stage decision is managing a stage boundary.
whyNot.2: Key decisions with delegated daily control describe directing a project.

A.q: What is the purpose of the 'initiating a project' process?
options: To lay solid foundations before significant expenditure
To confirm that the prerequisites for initiation exist
To confirm acceptance of the project product
To review the updated release map at a stage end
A.why: Initiating a project establishes solid foundations so the business understands the work needed before committing significant expenditure or resources (13.4.1).

whyNot.1: Checking the prerequisites for initiation is the purpose of starting up a project.
whyNot.2: Confirming acceptance of the project product is closing a project.
whyNot.3: Reviewing the updated release map is part of managing a stage boundary.

B.q: Which process enables the project board to be accountable for success by making key decisions and exercising overall control, while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager?
B.why: That is the purpose of directing a project (13.3.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage is the PM's day-to-day management of the stage.
whyNot.1: A stage boundary supplies the board with information; the decisions are taken in directing.
whyNot.3: Initiating builds the foundations for the project before significant expenditure.

B.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. The purpose of the [?] process is to assign work, monitor it, handle issues, report progress to the board and take corrective action so the stage stays within tolerance.
B.why: This is the purpose of controlling a stage (13.5.1).

whyNot.1: Managing product delivery controls the link between the PM and the delivery team.
whyNot.2: Managing a stage boundary informs the board's review of the stage and the next stage plan.
whyNot.3: Directing a project is the board's process of key decisions and overall control.

B.q:
Which two statements about the processes are correct?
1. Managing a stage boundary gives the board information to approve the next stage plan.
2. Closing a project is run as its own stage after the final delivery stage.
3. Controlling a stage can be used during initiation for large or complex projects.
4. Starting up a project is where significant expenditure is committed.
B.why: A stage boundary lets the board approve the next stage plan (13.7.1), and controlling a stage can be used in initiation on large or complex projects (13.5.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: closing a project is part of the final stage, not a stage of its own.
whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: closing happens inside the final stage.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: closing is not a stage, and starting up comes before any significant expenditure.

C.q: Which process gives the board the information it needs to confirm continued business justification before the next stage, and what acts as the next stage plan?
options: Controlling a stage; the team plan
Managing a stage boundary; the updated release map
Initiating a project; the project brief
Directing a project; the exception report
C.why: Managing a stage boundary lets the board review the stage, approve the next stage plan as an updated release map and confirm justification and risks (13.7.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage keeps the current stage on track; team plans cover an iteration.
whyNot.2: The project brief is assembled in starting up, not at a stage boundary.
whyNot.3: Directing is where the board decides; an exception report is for forecast tolerance breaches.

C.q: A mandate arrives. The PM must first check the idea is viable and worthwhile, and then build foundations before major spend. Which two processes are these, in order?
options: Initiating a project, then controlling a stage
Directing a project, then initiating a project
Starting up a project, then initiating a project
Starting up a project, then managing a stage boundary
C.why: Starting up asks 'viable and worthwhile?' (13.2.1); initiating lays foundations before significant expenditure (13.4.1).

whyNot.0: Initiating comes second, after starting up has checked viability.
whyNot.1: Directing is the board's process, not the check on viability.
whyNot.3: The second step builds foundations, which is initiating, not a stage boundary.

C.q: Which management level does managing product delivery belong to, and who carries it out in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Delivering level; the PO and delivery team
C.why: Managing product delivery is the delivering level: the product owner (a version of the team manager) and the delivery team (13.6.1).

whyNot.0: The PM works at the managing level in processes such as controlling a stage.
whyNot.1: The project board works at the directing level in directing a project.
whyNot.2: The agile coach supports agile adoption across the organization; it is not a process level.

reteach.title: Opening a new library branch
reteach.question: How would a council open a new library branch using the seven processes?

blocks.h: Same questions, in the same order
blocks.body: First the council asks whether a branch is worth exploring at all (starting up). Then it plans properly before signing the lease (initiating). Councillors make the big calls along the way (directing). The branch manager runs each phase (controlling a stage), the fitters and IT team build it (managing product delivery), each phase is reviewed before the next is funded (stage boundary), and finally the keys are handed over (closing).

blocks.caption: Councillors direct throughout: directing a project.

blocks.text: Handing over the keys happens inside the last phase; there is no separate 'closing phase'.

explain.body: Starting up a project begins with the project mandate from the business layer. It checks the prerequisites for initiation by asking whether the project is viable and worthwhile.

test.q: What triggers the 'starting up a project' process?
test.why: The project mandate, whatever information triggers the project, starts the process (13.2.1).

whyNot.1: The PID is assembled in initiating a project, later.
whyNot.2: The project brief is an output of starting up, approved by the board.
whyNot.3: The release map for initiation is produced during starting up.

explain.body: Directing a project belongs to the project board. The board stays accountable through key decisions and overall control, and delegates day-to-day management to the PM within tolerances.

test.q: In which process does the project board make key decisions and exercise overall control?
test.why: Directing a project is the board's process (13.3.1).

whyNot.0: Starting up is mostly the PM's work, checking viability.
whyNot.1: Controlling a stage is the PM's day-to-day process.
whyNot.3: Closing is prepared by the PM; the board authorizes closure in directing.

explain.body: Controlling a stage is the PM assigning and monitoring work and correcting deviations. Managing product delivery is the delivery side: the team accepts, executes and reports on work, linking the PM and the delivery team.

test.q: Which process controls the link between the project manager and the delivery team?
test.why: Managing product delivery controls that link through agreed requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery (13.6.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage is the PM assigning and monitoring work for the stage.
whyNot.2: A stage boundary prepares the board's next stage decision.
whyNot.3: Initiating lays foundations before significant spend.

explain.body: At each stage end, managing a stage boundary prepares the updated release map and dashboard for the board. Closing a project, inside the final stage, is the fixed point where acceptance of the project product is confirmed.

test.q: Which process provides a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed?
test.why: Closing a project is the fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed (PRINCE2 7 manual 19.1; Agile book 13.8).

whyNot.0: A stage boundary reviews a stage and approves the next stage plan.
whyNot.1: In directing, the board authorizes closure, but the confirmation work happens in closing.
whyNot.2: Controlling a stage manages the work of a stage.
